utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Sir, can an ordinary person -- and when I say "an ordinary person" I mean someone who has not been trained in military things -- could he distinguish by hearing such or such shell, oh, this is an 82, this is a 62, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would depend on how many that person may have heard before because on identifying mortars by sound there is no substitute for experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Quite. But let us imagine that people are -- don't have experience and that they hear not very frequently such firing near from where they were fired, would it be possible for them to identify them; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the person has not heard many rounds fired or has not been there long, it would be difficult for him to tell the difference between probably a medium or heavy mortar. However, most people should know the difference between a light mortar and a heavy mortar because their noise is vastly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And do you think that such a difference for ordinary people would be distinguishable at a distance of say two kilometres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that depends on the person, his experience. But an untrained person would probably have difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir I think that you went on mission -- different missions in Kenya. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I ask you who did -- who contracted you to go there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The British government have an agreement with the Kenyan government for the British Army to train in Kenya every year and because of that, obviously, safety has to be set up. And I was employed by half of the British government to act as the senior safety officer for those particular exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your written statement that in Kenya, ground was particularly dry, compact and hard.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And that you considered this as being a -- not a soft ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not. It was very hard ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the state of the tail-fins, if you had fired rounds, what was the state of the tail-fins that you may have found in C-2?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the hardness of the ground, a low percentage of the tail-fins are located in the craters. Of those that did locate in the crater, the base of the tail-fins were normally bent backwards because of the firmness of the ground, and they were located in the ground anything from only a couple of centimetres to being, some of them a few centimetres under ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: These deformed tail-fins, were they slightly deformed or quite severely deformed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were just slightly deformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you said that they had only penetrated slightly into the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was some of them. Some had penetrated below ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you also went on mission to Germany?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I think that you also fired on tarmac ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And what was the degree of deformation on tail-fins in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, it was an incident which I had to investigate not normal firing. There were five rounds fired. Only two of the craters had the tail-fins in them. In that particular case, as far as I can remember they were both approximately down to ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. But in relation to the deformation of tail-fins, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the hard ground they were obviously bent back. Once we retrieved them, there was damage on the end of the tail-fin and also some of the fins were bent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say that they were bent back, does it mean that the tail-fins were practically folded back towards the tail?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I say fold, the shaft or section of the tail-fin was obviously deformed backwards, as it had been driven into the ground. But the tail-fins were more bent to one side rather than bent backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, in your opinion, would using a small charge, would this add precision to firing or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this I take it you mean using one of the lower charges to fire the mortar?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For instance, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, the least charge you can place on the mortar, the better the accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, what about if the charges themselves are old? If these charges are already old or older, would this have any bearing on the accuracy of firing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can do with certain old charges if they get wet, they can deteriorate and produce shorter ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For instance the fact that if ammunition is left outside without protection, is this something that would influence the accuracy of firing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was to occur, then certain types of the older ammunitions can be affected by damp and weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, I would like to come back to the -- to the firing in salvo, that is, in rapid firing, you defined this type of firing as being harassment fire. I believe that is what you said, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. The -- if you were going to try and, what we call "neutralise" the target, you would fire a number of rounds in quick succession. If, however, you are just harassing the target, you normally fire less rounds over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, let us imagine that we are in the following situation: Where a target is small, small groups of people are moving in order to -- for a change of shift, and small groups of people are together in front -- standing together in front of an entrance to a building or waiting to get into a vehicle, hypothetically speaking, two or three rounds that are targeted are they justifiable from a military point of view, in order not to waste ammunition; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The size of target is always taken into account. You always try and fire the minimum amount of ammunition to achieve your aim. So for a group, let's say, of just half a dozen or ten people, with a medium mortar, you would probably limit that to three rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Sir, if I have a specific particular geographic situation with before me material obstacles, for instance, which would be a whole wall of high-rise buildings which would prevent me from seeing the location of the battle, if behind that wall of the building there is something which I believe to be a group of soldiers or people who are armed, therefore, targets, could I -- so I would be able to fire on them and hit them with a mortar round; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would be able to hit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir I would like to ask you a couple of more questions on the basis of photos --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this surprised me to the extent that it was indicated that the time available would be over now. I will give you another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite, thank you, Mr. President. With the assistance of the usher, could you please come over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please assist, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to place these photos on the ELMO, three photos. No. Two photos, plus a couple of others as well. No. Two photos. I correct myself. And meanwhile, if we could get the picture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exhibit, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is -- the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The ERN number is 00 --

utterances.text: We have no ERN numbers available to the Bench, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to check this. I think they have not been submitted by the Prosecution yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not yet been tendered and admitted. Are they not part of other P Exhibits which --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, well. Mr. President, I can quite simply put them on the ELMO. This seems to me a policy which is acceptable on occasion, and not tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I take it that I see from a distance, that these photographs are part of perhaps a report or a photo series, and then, of course, we cannot just put them on the ELMO and say "just look at this photograph but I am not going to tell you from which document it comes." I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the origin of these pictures is a document I don't have a title for because I was in Geneva tending to other business. I do have the ERN number for the Prosecution, if I can I will, and if I can't I will move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where it comes from, otherwise the other party could not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but these pictures come from the Prosecution. There is a number there 00269225. 00269773. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please first give them to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is just the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the Prosecution this is part -- have you identified what documents we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The numbers seem to be incorrect, the numbers that were given --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I give up the idea. I give up altogether. There is an ERN number, so it's perfectly, apparently, it is not, but I give up altogether. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you just would have indicated what is on the front page on the series of photographs, then it would have been easy I take it to -- for the Prosecution to identify what document that is. utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that I have got in front of me, well, for the sake of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a document which comes from the Prosecution, part of the photo documentation, I have got it in Serbian, PredMet shelling location the street of Rade Koncara or rather the square of Rade Koncara, Sarajevo, the date when the photo was taken, the 9th of November, 1993. I would have liked for this picture, bearing the number 225, to be submitted to the expert. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put it on the ELMO, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is P1386, but I am really not sure, so I am not even going to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, can you see here --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the speakers speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: A crater on a hard surface?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you see here what we normally call a burrow -- a fuse furrow?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see one from that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true sir, that when a 120 millimetre mortar hits a certain spot, generally speaking, the area around the crater and the crater itself are cleared of all debris?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just pose the question again, please? I don't understand the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it not true sir, that when a 120 millimetre shell explodes, the crater itself is totally cleared of debris, it is blown away, the debris is blown away?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of debris will be blown away, but as far as we have already discussed, sometimes the tail-fin will be there, sometimes the fuse, and if the crater is deep enough, sometimes you will get some of the shrapnel parts from the top of the body will sometimes still be in the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Apart from the parts of the shell and the tail-fin, anything else, that is to say anything that might have been either around or within the crater, is it not true that it would be blown away by the blast of the explosion and that the crater itself would be clear, cleared of all debris? Apart from the tail-fin and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially that can be the way. But because of the way the blast works it is sometimes possible for an article to be blown up into the air which of course settles back down on top of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My very last question, sir, when you submitted your expertise, were you told that the Serb forces on the one hand had relatively old bombs and armaments, weapons, in general, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a consequence were you given any indication or any information as to the various models of the bombs used by the Serb side; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not given any of that information. I have most of that information as part of my work anyway back in my office in the UK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see the interpreters, when you indicated your last question, already translated as your very last question, but that is perhaps because the words get a different meaning now and then. Is there any need to cross-examine the witness Mr. Ierace -- to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like the witness to do a diagram, perhaps the witness can be given a sheet of paper and a pen. I have a sheet of paper and a pen, if you can't locate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you have been asked a number of questions about the profile of the fuse adapter. You have told us that certain parts were vertical and other parts not. Could you please do a cross section of an adapter showing us which parts are vertical and which parts are not. And after you have done that, could you please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Would you please now explain the diagram, now that we can see it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have there, you can see that the adapter, it's outer dimensions, a conical-shaped to follow the curve of the body of the round. It has two threads. The bottom one, which is that one there, is what screws it into the top of the body of the round. The inner one up here, which normally fits inside a centre chamber is the one which the screw, the screw thread of the fuse will fit into so the fuse then will fit down into the centre cylinder.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the photograph that you marked on Friday --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that is P3741, might that be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that the one which has the pen markings on it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Could you briefly place that on the ELMO above the diagram. Now I am going to ask you to indicate on your diagram where you think the piece you have marked as number "1" may have come from.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one, due to its slightly larger diameter, has possibly come from somewhere on one of the sides towards the base of the adapter due to its slightly large diameter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please take a blue pen and mark on your diagram the area from where number 1 may possibly have come from, and put a "1" alongside that blue-marked area.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I think you indicated the exterior edge in your explanation. Could you mark with the blue pen the relevant edge with number 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the part where it is possible where this piece came from towards the outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now please place, if the court usher could place the photograph back on the ELMO so that we can all remind ourselves of piece number two, would you please now indicate on the diagram where piece number two may have come from, in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to its slightly smaller diameter, it has either come from the same side, from just above number one, or, of course, from anywhere around the circumference of the fuse adapter. So just for diagraphic sakes, I pill put it on the same side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please now return to the photograph, Mr. Usher, so we can all see number 3. Yes. Thank you. Would you please now indicate where you say, in your opinion, piece number three may have come from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Piece number three, of course, is not shown on this diagram, as that resembles the fuse cover on the end of the fuse, which would normally be located when it was screwed into position at the end of the fuse which would protrude out of the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please place a cross and a number three in the area that you now indicate with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That might now be taken away. I will tender that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, on Friday, you were asked a question do the effect of whether you had been shown by the Prosecution a report which indicated in relation to shelling incident number five, that the fire could have come from either side of the confrontation line. And you said "the only reports I have seen are the forensic and the other ones which I have referred to in my report." Do you have a copy of your report with you at the moment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness -- perhaps we can do it from memory to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to shelling incident number five, did you indicate three sources of information, A, being technical examination report dated 8 February 1994, followed by an ERN number; B, UNPROFOR investigation report dated 15 February 1994 followed by an ERN number; and C, witness statement B supply dated 27th of February 1996; is that correct. Does that accord with your memory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I ask the witness be shown P2261 which has the same ERN number on page one, as appears in the witness's report alongside Reference B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is this a previously admitted document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, it is in fact the exhibit which I obtained earlier from Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, I have placed two yellow tabs on a document. Would you go to the first tab, that is the one closest to the first page, and look at the bottom of that page and could you please read the last sentence. Perhaps you could read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. "The distance of origin of fire clearly overlaps each side of the confrontation line by 2000 metres. Both parties are known --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Both parties are known to have 120 millimetre mortars and the bombs to go along with them. The team has no reason to believe that either party does not have access to the type of ammunition reported in paragraph 12. There is insufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb in question could have been fired by either side."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now in relation to the relation to the phrase "insufficient physical evidence" did the UNPROFOR investigation report consider the evidence extracted from the mortar crater and the immediate surrounds of the mortar impact point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From reading the report, the UNPROFOR team did their inspection a number of days after the original investigation was carried out, and they did not have all the evidence available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So I might now return D61 and from the bar table and also P2261A. I am grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could the report of Mr. Higgs be handed up to you. Please have a look on Annex A which is Captain Houdet, crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that actually is not part of the report of this witness, but rather part of the second filing on the 4th of June titled "Prosecutor's submission of addendum to the expert report of Richard Higgs." So I don't know whether the witness would have that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not in this one here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is P3734A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I am sorry, but in my papers, it is attached to the report. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: In the conclusions, it says, in number two, that at the minimum angle, the minimum range is 1.120 metres for 81 millimetre mortar and 1.340 metres for 120 millimetre mortar. In your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. opinion in this report, it is possible to conclude that at another angle the distance could be longer or shorter or.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be any longer, Your Honour. He has used the minimum angle of descent of 45 degrees to come up with a minimum range of 1120. That is the maximum range of the mortar. Minimum angle of descent gives maximum range. So to get a shorter range the angle of descent would be higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Has Captain Houdet says the angle of range and descent cannot be determined.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on this case there was no fuse furrow. He wasn't able to ascertain the accurate angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That is my question. Is it possible to have another angle of descent in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: If this is the minimum, is it possible to have a, let's say, maximum or intermediate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it is, Your Honour. This is the minimum of 45, but anywhere between there and approximately an angle of 85, 90 degrees, anywhere in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can we go to your report and I think that I am not wrong. Your report, page nine.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: When you are talking of, let's say the report on the incident of the 22nd of January the third paragraph, the second and third paragraphs, well what you are saying there is that your conclusion is different of that of Verdy because the Verdy report was done the next day.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And the conclusion of the forensic investigation is that two mortar bombs of 82 millimetres were fired and one of 120 millimetres landed on the other side of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, and Verdy says -- well you say that the data, I mean that this data do not make sense, 120 millimetres instead of 82 millimetres. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the crater analysis done by the forensic team at the time, the craters do not appear through their size and shape to be 120 millimetre craters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: But according to the forensic investigation report, three bombs were fired.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Two 82 millimetres and one 120 millimetre. All right. Thank you. Could you please have a look on the set of maps -- I think that -- this set of maps. I don't know which is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I don't have that number anywhere in my copy. Please go to the incident numbered three. We have two spots there, A and B. Which is the distance between those two spots?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Distance between the two falls of shot is just over 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Let's have a look on the origin of the red lines. Which is the distance between that place and the green line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately one thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Are we looking at the same place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the lines of fire, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Not the dotted line, but the hard line, the red hard line.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back along those lines to the force of shot it is approximately one thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Until the green line? Please show me. Not from there, from the beginning. From there to the next -- well, not the -- yes, to the left there is a green line. The distance -- not the other one. The red line and the green line close to it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No not from there from here.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there to there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: To the other side.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there across to there, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is approximately 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: 300 metres. I should say a little bit less because if the other one is 100, it is more or less the same distance. But anyway this -- this spot is the origin of the fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the direction it was given in the forensic report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So that is the place, well the supposed place from which the fire, the mortar was fired or the mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the help of the interpreters, we would like to conclude before the break. Judge El Mahdi has one question for you, and I might have one as well. And we will then have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Could you please go to page 10 and page 11 of your report. If we read that page 11, the very last paragraph, I am going to quote in English: [In English] "Possible to hit the market with a single initially sited round it is more likely to be the case if the target was prerecorded." [Interpretation] Can you see that? So my question is in relation to the following: You explained that this was not about -- just about calculating the angle of firing, but it should also take -- it should also be taken into consideration the weather conditions, wind, if I understand you correctly, and the temperature.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if you are firing from a distance at about 2 kilometres or more on an elevated ground, so the temperature would be higher than the centre of the city, what would be the accuracy, since you say that the probability is quite high, that a single shell would hit one target as long as it is prerecorded, as you say. So, in order to target an objective -- a target in the city with the weather conditions and the buildings that are high, medium height, temperature a little higher than where the temperature -- where the firing comes from, can you give us an approximation of on the hypothesis of the probabilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First thing, Your Honour, to be aware of, is the temperature is only taken at the firing position. Because it's the temperature that effects the burning speed of the propellant and effects the range. So temperature of the target is not taken into account. On the probability of hitting the target would depend upon when the target was last prerecorded, and if they had re-recorded if the weather had possibly changed. If a mortar had fired some time previous in the day or through the night and got more up-to-date information, then a target the size of the market, you would very easily hit with one round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By taking into consideration the wind, the force of wind, the strength which could change, it would be a favourable wind or not favourable wind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wind is always the one factor which must be taken into account because it can effect mortar rounds very badly. That is why, if you were going to try and engage this target, and you had not fired for some time, you would ideally want to fire some time that morning or some time before, because then you could calculate the errors the wind is giving you and then take them into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, let us assume that there was no firing during the day. So it was during the day or perhaps the previous night, there was no firing and the possibility, however, diminishes then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it does, Your Honour. But if you know what the weather conditions are, if you have a weather forecast of wind speed and direction, you can still calculate those figures into your calculation. It is not as accurate as being able to fire but it still means that your first round should land possibly within 100 metres of what you are firing at, straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have two questions for you. I will start with the first one in the meantime. Madam Registrar could you or Mr. Usher, wait for one second. I am taking you to page 12 of your report. The very last three lines where you say "this witness was in a good position to hear mortar fire in the vicinity." And then "if there was no other mortar fire at that particular time, it follows that the evidence of the hearing of the mortar being fired could be used to determine the likely location of its source." Could you explain this to me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the witness's location is in the lower ground, that high feature that we spoke about. Because of the direction that he spoke about, impossible to get range from that or an exact bearing from what he has said. But it helped me to eliminate the chance of a mortar being down the location where he was and possibly more towards the direction of the city. The direction that he ascertained put the mortar behind that high feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the first line "the witness was in a good position to hear mortar firing in the vicinity." Would that be true for everyone? I mean, if I would say that I am in a good position to hear mortar fire from my vicinity would that be always true or?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not always going to be true. The -- saying in his vicinity, the area that he was in below the escarpment, I used that information to try and eliminate the areas rather than locate precise areas. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it was in his vicinity.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was in his vicinity where he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a lot closer to him, he would have come up with a completely different direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now I do understand that if you say "it was really close to him" he would have heard that in a different way and therefore it would not have been that close.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I better understand you. Mr. Usher could you please, I sometimes make a sketch as well in order to clarify myself. Could it please be put on the ELMO. You explained to us that the two pieces you indicated on this photograph might have come from one, that would be the larger diameter or perhaps the other one from indicated two, the smaller diameter. But we were talking about the internal diameters and I pointed with two small arrows to -- as a matter of fact, I copied your sketch -- where I see no difference in internal diameters. So could you please explain how what you told us would be an explanation for the difference in internal diameters.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have shown on the drawing, Your Honour, is the outer part of the adapter is this part here which of course is cone shaped and gets smaller towards the top. But inside, there is a chamber, a fuse chamber which is shown by these parallel lines. This is separate to the adapter normally fitted inside. When the round explodes, this after will fragmentate and go somewhere different. So you are then left with the parallel chamber separating from the outer wall, which of course is a conical-shaped, so you would expect to see in the shrapnel, small pieces towards the top, larger pieces towards the bottom. If you are lucky enough to find any pieces from this part here, then they would have exactly the same internal diameter. But from the picture, I haven't seen any pieces that represent that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So are you telling us that the two vertical lines in the centre of the adapter would also indicate that these are different parts of materiel fitted in -- this is a separate part, yes. So what I suggested with my dotted line to the right that there might be differences in the interior of the adapter is to some extent true, although not in the way I suggested it by the dotted line, but that the upper part that we have -- well, it is still not quite clear to me, how this then functioned. You may, if you want to, adapt my -- because I still need a different internal diameter at X 1 and X 2.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different manufacturers of fuses of course have different designs for this. You have the parallel one which I show here where you have a separate like cylinder which screws into the inside. But sometimes you may find one which is wider at the top, cuts in and then goes down, which again would still give you the same problem with the shrapnel, you have thin pieces at the top and the larger pieces at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you do get parallel ones and you do get ones which have a step on them. It just depends on the type of manufacturer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so then can be in the same adapter different internal diameters according to their construction.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before you leave that, I intend to tender this sketch because of the value of the witness' responses. Because I respectfully suggest that some of the points which the witness has indicated be captured for the transcript, in particular, the last response of the witness indicating a step, could be indicated by the witness drawing that step onto the diagram rather than explaining it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although -- I copied it from the witness anyhow so there will be no intellectual rights as far as the drawing is concerned. You may indicate on this sketch what you just indicated to us. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that you said you had two questions. I don't know whether it was your last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the leave to ask another question in relation to what you have asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... matter which has been extensively dealt with by the Defence perhaps not completely so extensively, so one question -- so both your last and your very last question on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you know, yes or no, if the Yugoslav manufacturer had ever made weapons from which the adapter -- of which the adapter would have been composed of elements that would allow it to give two interior diameters on this relevant piece; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JAMES HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this will be a -- have you got a number in mind, Mr. Ierace. We will do that later. We will first have the break. Mr. Higgs, this concludes your examination in this court. I want to thank you for coming and answering all the questions both of the parties and of the Bench, and I hope that you will be in time for what you intended to do this afternoon. Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, would you escort Mr. Higgs out of the courtroom and we will have a break -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before we proceed with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Gavrankapetanovic, the Defence would like to ask for a few minutes after the next break in relation to an explanation regarding the decision of your Chamber in relation to Rule 92 bis when we are talking about the examination-in-chief of Mr. Gavrankapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break until 10 minutes past 1.00 and the apologise of the Chamber for the long time this part of the session took. The shorter will be the next one. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I suggest that we first deal with the documents regarding Mr. Higgs, that I will then give you the opportunity to ask or tell us what you have in mind. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we do the documents, might I make a quick observation in relation to the questions asked by Judge Nieto-Navia in relation to distances on that map. Might I remind you of evidence from this witness in relation to the ability to measure distances on the coloured maps, as opposed to the black and white map. The black and white map can be used accurately, but not the coloured ones, because the grids are not square. Rather than waste time with re-examination, I thought I would simply point out that earlier evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is some perspective distortion in these maps. Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am surprised by this kind of observation. This is something we know. This is a waste of time, and this is the best demonstration of the fact that these maps are not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope that, as a matter of fact, this was to some extent a comment on a witness statement which could have perhaps better we addressed at a later stage when we have to evaluate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could indicate exactly where this could be found, Mr. Ierace, then the Chamber would like to have the source. On the other hand, in general I would say comment on witness statements, this is not the appropriate time to do it. But, you immediately took over and commented on it as well saying that it was -- the maps are not right. I think we should save argument for the appropriate moment. But the information asked for, we will receive that from Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is Exhibit P3644 RH which also shows the green lines and the directions of fire. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you guide us through the documents in relation to the expert witness, Mr. Higgs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed, Mr. Ierace, that you did not only intend to tender my last copied sketch but even some others which I invented entirely myself. But that is not the issue. If you would like to do so, perhaps do that now, so that we can deal with it when going through the documents tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I seek to tender MFI 13, 14 and 15. 15 in particular, I think it was, was a subject of comment by the witness and therefore the appropriate evidentiary base is laid. That would be exhibits P3744, P3745, and P3746.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 3744, 45, and 46 and I think we already have a number for the sketch with the adapter. So then, please, Madam Registrar, would you assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3734A, Prosecutor's submission of addendum to the expert report of Richard Higgs; Exhibit P3734A.1, B/C/S translation; Exhibit P3734, expert report; Exhibit P3734.1, B/C/S translation; Exhibit P3741, picture marked by witness; Exhibit P3742, diagram drawn and marked by witness; Exhibit P3743, diagram; Exhibit P3744, document previously marked for identification number 13; Exhibit P3745, document previously marked for identification number 14; Exhibit P3746, document previously marked for identification number 15; Exhibit P3644.RH, map marked by witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President in relation to these maps and in particular this map, the Defence intends to make an objection for the following reason: That is, that in this case, the locations of the areas where the firing came from are certainly important and this type of exercise should be done before the Chamber, particularly when we are talking about the areas that are close to combat lines. By just giving information from one side which, when we are talking about people who are experts, I don't think that this is done fairly and I believe that we are not coming close enough to the truth. That is the reason why this map, having been pre-marked by the witness on the basis of some information that were given to him by the Prosecution only, and we did see that some of the information given did not relate to the actual firing tables and that is what the witness himself had said. And I don't think that they can be accepted as such. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general, the Chamber accepts the pre-marked maps if they are marked by that witness, if they have been disclosed in time, if there has been an opportunity to cross-examine the witness on the correctness of the markings he made. And, of course, the Chamber will have to assess finally the probative value of the markings on the maps. So the objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D167, picture of grenade and fuse; Exhibit D168 drawing of adapter; D169, picture of adapters; D170, photocopy of a portion of D169.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to so much of those four documents which has not been explained or the subject of evidence. In that regard, I especially object to virtually everything on D170. The only question that was asked of the witness in relation to that diagram was for him to confirm that the external size of the item marked by "A" is smaller than the item marked by "B." No basis of the circles or other calculations or even other diagrams on that sheet was explained or the subject of cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. To exclude these exhibits that would really not to want to have the truth exposed. The truth is that there are two pieces and the inside -- internal comparisons are obviously not the same -- I am just answering, thank you. I am not going to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there is an objection of a technical nature. And of course I do understand that both parties will only tender those documents that would pertain to the truth, I mean, otherwise, that means I would deal with nonprofessionals, so that needs no explanation. The technical issue, I would like to have your response on that because that is what the Chamber has to decide upon, not whether you are, at this moment, trying to seek the truth with these documents because that goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, therefore, I will continue from where I stopped. These pieces, these exhibits establish a fact which is the difference in diameter on two elements that were formally identified by this expert witness as being the pieces of the adapter. And these pieces show what is the adapter and what is its position on the shell how an adapter looks when it is presented in cross section, and on the basis of the photographs that we were given, what are the radius differences, that is, the differences in diameter. Now, Mr. President, if tomorrow our expert comes to confirm and to claim that there was only one type of fuse in the Yugoslav Army, that is, one single type with a vertical chamber, and not with a different type of chamber, then it will be definitely established that there are two internal diameters while theoretically there should only be one. And these are -- these exhibits are just the beginning of demonstrating this evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say the importance is the demonstration of the difference in diameter and that is the only thing the witness testified about. I think the complaint was that the Chamber should only admit these documents to the extent that they indicate a difference in internal diameter. So that is, as a matter of fact, is mainly a matter of assessing the probative value of the documents and not much more than that. So therefore, the Chamber will admit into evidence these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. President, but the diagram of the shell is not just showing this difference in diameter, but also the exact position of the adapter, that could be only just one diameter possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this last part is a comment. But the documents are the -- the Chamber will assess the probative value of these documents and they are admitted into evidence. Being there are no other objections, all the other documents just mentioned by Madam Registrar admitted into evidence as well. Ms. Pilipovic, you would like to address the Chamber in view of the testimony of the witness Gavrankapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am going to do it instead of my colleague, Mr. President. It seems to us that the testimony of the witness, and I have conferred with my colleague earlier, and I read the beginning of the examination this morning, it seems to us that this intervention goes beyond the framework that was given by your order of the 26th of July 2002 by stating the conditions of application of Rule 92 bis in relation to this witness as well, and that were supposed to guarantee to us about half an hour of maximum of cross-examination. And this is for this file, which was clearly marked in your decision. Now I believe that we -- this has gone well beyond this. There were many questions asked and a number of victims in Markale and so on, and the Defence has some questions, the Defence is wondering, that is what we wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gavrankapetanovic is not testifying in this court on the base of 92 bis. His statement has not been admitted into evidence. I think the major issue is that Mr. Gavrankapetanovic was presented in writing as an authenticating witness and being called as a viva voce witness, his testimony goes beyond what is authentication of documents. And, as a matter of fact, I see that the Prosecution is seeking admission into evidence of other documents, not those documents specifically mentioned and also dealt with in our decision that were or were not in need of any further authentification. So, therefore, the half of hour, of course, is not valid because this is not the way of presenting the evidence. So I would say the general rule applies. Could we then continue the examination of Mr. Gavrankapetanovic. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness in. It will be very short, but I would nevertheless like to -- perhaps, I am wondering, there is another issue we have to deal with first. And it might not be of any use any more to -- but let's see. General Galic, as I indicated before, there would be a possibility to sit on Thursday longer than usual. Your counsel have indicated that you -- that your health situation would not -- would be such that we at least first should consult you to see what would be possible for you. And I would like to know what would approximately be -- approximately be the limits. So we are not talking about the whole week, every day, we are just talking about Thursday and extending the hours. Then I will say it will then be considerably -- would a normal day be approximately four and a half hours in court apart from the breaks. That would be then, well, let's say, at least six, perhaps even seven. I would like to hear your views on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour, and thank you for consulting me as to the length of the hearing for Thursday. That's my understanding, that you refer to Thursday only. Well, I can tell you that in spite of everything, I did my best in trying to keep up so far, and with the help of the doctors and the medicines, it is functioning. To what extent, well, I don't know, but apparently it is working at the moment. I would tend to say that is a bit too long. I am not at all certain, considering the way I feel today, and I mean, you know these things may change. Sometimes I am in no pain at all and on others days I don't feel quite so good. As to whether I will be sufficiently well on Thursday to be able to stay here for such a long time, well, if I feel I am not up to it, I will let you know. I hope you will allow me. But if there is no choice, and if that is your decision, for us to stay here all day on Thursday, I will do my best. I will try and be here. Well, thank you. I mean I have nothing else to say at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Galic, it is not a hard decision at this moment as you will have heard, the Prosecution asked to seek additional time this week and we try to find it, but we have not yet decided. That is exactly the reason why I am asking you. There would be a -- there would be a possibility of various approaches. One would be, let's just start on Thursday and see how far we come and if you say, no, I really now need a break, and then to say or that you say, this is for today is the maximum I can do, that would be a way of just seeing where we come and starting on Thursday. Another opportunity would be, and then of course, I would have to look first at the Prosecution, to see whether there are specific aspects of the case presentation which could be dealt with in such a way, for example, that you could follow it, perhaps not in the courtroom, but visually and by audio but in a more comfortable position. That would still ask your concentration, but would not ask your position in sitting and perhaps giving -- giving your back a bit more rest so you might be in a different literal position then. So I am trying to find out what would be possible. If you would say, and if you would look at the second option, then I would like to know who exactly has been scheduled for the second part of Thursday. If you say "no, I prefer to see how far we can come on Thursday," then, of course, I would not and the Chamber would not have to enquire into the schedule of the Prosecutor for Thursday because then we will just start and you will indicate where you would need an additional break or where you would say, "well, this is what my physical condition allows me" and we will carefully listen to you. So I am thinking of one of these two approaches. Would you have yourself any preference, that you would say, well, if we would try to sit more on Thursday I would prefer to be present and indicate when I would like to have an extra break; or to indicate where my physical condition does not allow me any more to follow the proceedings; or would you rather say could we find a solution where I could follow from a distance with perhaps a possibility of communication with counsel or intermediatory communication with counsel. Then of course I would have to explore the possibilities, but, would you have any preference?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what sort of communication are you suggesting? Because you can tell that the communication channels are open between us and, well if we want to give you a red light, so to say, it would be a bit difficult. So what sort of communication do you intend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment it is not a matter of give the right light -- the green light, I would say to the Chamber, or the red light, but we could consider that. Of course, we would like not to have any -- any communication between here and the place where General Galic would be. I am first asking for the preference. I asked General Galic what his preference would be and then, according to his preference, we would like to further investigate what would be possible. So may I ask you what your preference would be, General Galic, to give it a try and see where we come, or to -- that we try to create specific conditions that, even outside the courtroom, you might be able to follow the proceedings, but in a more comfortable position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am a soldier and I prefer simple solutions. The simplest solution would be to be present here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then see where we come?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe my answer was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will take that into consideration when giving a decision on the schedule for next Thursday. Thank you very much. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have received an understanding, we understand that Ewa Tabeau wishes to know whether she will be recalled. I think she might be anxious to be dismissed because of other reasons. Is the Trial Chamber in a position at this stage to indicate definitely one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the Defence agree with excusing Madam Tabeau? I see one Defence counsel nodding "yes" and the other one "no," but it must have different meanings. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague and myself have decided to cross-examine the witness and it would take up to 15 or 20 minutes. It could be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence must have a chance to cross-examine Ewa Tabeau on the additional part of her report. You asked for 15 to 20 minutes. The Chamber takes it that you could perform that in 15 minutes, Ms. Pilipovic. And that would be an appropriate time in view of the material presented. Is there anything else at this very moment? If not, we will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.
